svg.text: Newborn jaundice: when the colour matters and when it does not
Jaundice in the first 24 hours
ALWAYS pathological. Never observe it.
Think haemolysis: rhesus or ABO
incompatibility, or G6PD deficiency,
which is common in Ghana.
Refer the same day for bilirubin level,
blood group, Coombs test and G6PD screen.
Jaundice from day 2 to day 5
Usually physiological — the newborn liver
is still slow to conjugate bilirubin, and
foetal red cells are being broken down.
Feed frequently, watch the level of the
yellowing, and review.
Still yellow after 14 days needs investigation.
Reading the level of the yellow — it descends head to toe
Face only — lowest levels · Chest and upper abdomen — rising · Below the umbilicus — higher
Palms and soles yellow — severe, refer immediately
Press the skin with your thumb and release, and look at the blanched skin in daylight, not under a bulb.
Kernicterus is permanent brain damage from unconjugated bilirubin, and it is entirely preventable by acting early.
Danger signs in a newborn — any one means refer urgently
Not feeding well or refusing the breast · Convulsions · Fast breathing over 60 a minute
Severe chest indrawing · Temperature 37.5 or above, or below 35.5 · Movement only on stimulation
Yellow palms and soles · Red or draining umbilicus with skin spreading · Ten or more skin pustules
A newborn who is simply not feeding is a sick newborn. It is the earliest sign of sepsis and it is easy to dismiss.
Cord care: keep it clean, dry and uncovered. Chlorhexidine 7.1 percent gel where the policy specifies it. Nothing else.
